name: La Bombonera
label: La Bombonera
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brandsen y Del Valle Iberlucea' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Brandsen and Del Valle Iberlucea (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/248598885: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'La Bombonera' (261 m across).
notes: Boca Juniors' famous stadium.

text.description:
La Bombonera is Boca Juniors' stadium in the La Boca neighbourhood, and its name means 'the chocolate box'. The nickname stuck after a third tier was completed in 1953, giving the stands their boxy, steep shape. The stadium opened on 25 May 1940. In 1996 a fourth tier was added, bringing capacity to 57,500. Outside, murals show everyday life in La Boca, which makes the walls as interesting to photograph as the structure.

This spot is the corner of Brandsen y Del Valle Iberlucea, on the stadium's west side. Boca's earlier ground stood on this same corner from 1924, before the present stadium replaced it. The corner gives a wider, more sideways view than the classic front-on shot. You see the curved stands and the flank of the ground, and one stand can look cut off at the edge. Treat it as an alternative angle rather than the postcard view. It works best if you like the stadium's odd, layered shape and want a different picture from the usual entrance shot. If you want the main street-side facade and entrance, with other visitors photographing from the pavement, walk round to the front of the stadium.

The stadium is large, so step back as far as is safe to fit it in. Look for the curve of the stands against the sky and keep the vertical lines straight. A planned expansion on the Del Valle Iberlucea side could change this view in future.
text.geographic_location: In the La Boca neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, on the streets directly around the Boca Juniors stadium. The spot is the corner of Brandsen and Del Valle Iberlucea, at the stadium's west side.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is given for this spot, so head for the La Boca neighbourhood and go by taxi or ride-hail to the corner of Brandsen and Del Valle Iberlucea. Once you are the middle of the stadium is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. Ask your driver for 'La Bombonera' and ask to be dropped at Brandsen y Del Valle Iberlucea. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the curved stands in from close range. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched picture. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the stand edges or a mural.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Brandsen and Del Valle Iberlucea (corner at the stadium's west side). A wider view of the stadium's curved stands and the side of the ground, with one stand appearing cut off at the corner. The stadium's centre lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a stand edge up with a vertical grid line so the building does not lean. Let the curve of the stands lead across the frame. Keep a bit of street in the foreground for scale. If you want the main facade and entrance with visitors in front, walk round to the street side instead and use the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stands to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stand details don't wash out. Hold the phone level to keep the lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime on a day with no match, when the streets are quieter and easier to stand in.

text.access_note: The corner is an ordinary street, but going inside the stadium or its museum is ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The corner of Brandsen and Del Valle Iberlucea is an ordinary public street that can be visited from outside.
Streets around the stadium are busier and may be restricted on match days.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit a large building into the frame when you are standing close.
A quiet, non-match daytime visit is the easiest time to stand and take photos at the corner.
Taxi or ride-hail is a practical way to reach the corner.

name: Teatro Colón
label: Teatro Colón
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza Lavalle' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza Lavalle' (relation/454905): middle (396 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23633911: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Teatro Colón' (132 m across).
notes: World-famous opera house.

text.description: The Teatro Colón is Buenos Aires' grand opera house, and from Plaza Lavalle you see the front facade and dome framed across the square. The theatre took about twenty years to build and opened on 25 May 1908 with Verdi's Aida. The sculpted busts and bas-reliefs on the facade are by Luigi Trinchero, and they reward a closer look with your zoom. The building was declared a National Historic Monument in 1989. It then closed for a long refurbishment from 2006 and reopened in May 2010. It has a reputation as one of the world's great opera houses, partly because of its acoustics, though you will not see that from outside. From there the theatre lies to the south-east, and the open square lets you fit the whole width of the building into one frame. One guide (Buenos Tours) treats the Avenida 9 de Julio side as the back and the Libertad/Plaza Lavalle side as the front, so check on the day. If you have time for one more angle, one guide suggests the corner of Cerrito and Tucumán for the full height of the facade and dome. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and wait for a gap in the people crossing the square.
text.geographic_location: The Teatro Colón is in central Buenos Aires, on Libertad street facing Plaza Lavalle.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Plaza Lavalle in the city centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the facade and dome across the square. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or trees block the full width. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues, busts and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Lavalle (front (Libertad side) of the theatre). The theatre's front facade and dome, framed from across the square. Try not to stand too close to the building, or you will have to tilt the phone upwards and the walls will lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them. Keep the dome near the top of the frame with a little sky above it. Use a tree or the edge of the square as a natural frame if one is handy. For a different view, one guide suggests the corner of Cerrito and Tucumán for the full height of the facade, and the Avenida 9 de Julio side offers another perspective on the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in a row, as people often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, when the facade is evenly lit, is the easiest time to photograph it. Early morning is usually quieter on the square. After dark, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: You can photograph the exterior from the public square; for tours or performances inside, check the official site before you go.

name: Recoleta Cemetery
label: Recoleta Cemetery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cementerio de la Recoleta' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cementerio de la Recoleta' (way/183842128): middle (438 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/183842128: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Recoleta Cemetry' (439 m across).
notes: Ornate mausoleums including Eva Perón's tomb.

text.description:
Recoleta Cemetery is a small city of tombs in the Recoleta neighbourhood. It began in 1822 as the first public cemetery in Buenos Aires, laid out in the old garden of a convent whose church, Our Lady of the Pillar, dates from 1732. Today it covers about 5.5 hectares and holds 4691 vaults, all above ground. Ninety-four of them are protected National Historical Monuments. The layout works like a set of city blocks, with wide tree-lined walkways branching into narrower lanes packed with marble mausoleums in Art Deco, Art Nouveau, Baroque and Neo-Gothic styles.

It photographs well because the first view is already a composition. You enter through neoclassical gates with tall Doric columns, and the ironwork and stone frame the lanes and tombs beyond. Once inside, the repeating rooflines and statues give you plenty of close-up subjects. The Gothic tomb of Liliana Crociati de Szaszak is of special interest because of its unusual design. A small colony of stray cats lives here too, about a dozen as of 2024.

Start at the entrance, then work inwards. Take a wide frame first, then move on to details such as statues, doors and carved stone. Be quiet and discreet around anyone visiting a grave, and don't climb on or touch the monuments.
text.geographic_location: Recoleta Cemetery is in the Recoleta neighbourhood of Buenos Aires. It is built around the old convent and the church of Our Lady of the Pillar.
text.directions_text: Head for the Recoleta neighbourhood and the cemetery. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The main entrance on the Junín side is a good first stop for a wide photo of the portico before you head in. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the whole entrance portico with the lanes beyond. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close to the columns and want to fit them all in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues, carvings and rooftops without leaning over anything.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (main entrance portico, Junín side). The neoclassical Doric-columned entrance framing the cemetery's tree-lined lanes and mausoleums beyond. From here, look along the tree-lined lanes towards the mausoleums.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a column or the gate with a vertical line so the portico stands straight. Let the ironwork and columns form a frame around the lane beyond. For a different subject, the Gothic tomb of Liliana Crociati, with its statue of a woman in a wedding dress beside her dog, suits close-up shots. The Claustros del Pilar are said to give an overhead view across the tomb tops, but check whether they are open to visitors before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or a column to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Keep flash off, especially near chapels. Portrait mode can work for statues if you stay at a respectful distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light gives good shadows on the gate.

text.access_note: Access and any entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide shots taken very close to the columns may stretch or tilt the edges of the frame.
The sky can look brighter than the shaded lanes beneath the trees, so lowering the exposure slider may help.
The area around Evita's tomb is usually crowded, so the entrance is a calmer place to take photos.

name: Casa Rosada
label: Casa Rosada
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Mayo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Mayo' (relation/17076039): middle (244 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/185738988: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pink House' (138 m across).
notes: The pink presidential palace.

text.description:
The Casa Rosada, or 'the pink house', is the Argentine president's official workplace and one of the best-known buildings in Buenos Aires. It stands at the eastern end of the Plaza de Mayo, the big square that has been the centre of the city's public life since the city was founded in 1580. The pink was reportedly chosen under President Sarmiento, and the building reached its present form in 1898 after it was enlarged and joined to the neighbouring Central Post Office. It is a National Historic Monument.

It photographs well because the square is wide and open, so you can step back and get the whole long facade in one frame. The Pirámide de Mayo, the obelisk-like monument in the middle of the plaza, makes a good foreground anchor and gives the picture some depth. This is the classic postcard view. Walk a little to one side and you get a more angled shot of the facade, often with fewer people in it.

Shoot from outside, as interior tours are no longer offered. A long fence has sometimes been put up across the plaza and can block your angle, so have a look when you arrive. On national holidays the building may be lit in different colours at night. If you want a view from above, the Cabildo across the square gives a higher angle with the Casa Rosada in the background, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Buenos Aires, at the eastern end of the Plaza de Mayo. Parque Colón lies directly behind the building.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for the Plaza de Mayo in the historic centre. From there the Casa Rosada is about 3 minutes on foot, and you will see it straight ahead. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole facade with the pyramid in front of it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building feels cut off at the sides or you want more of the square and sky. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the balcony and the flags.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Mayo (central part of the square, facing east, with the Pirámide de Mayo in the foreground). The pink facade of the Casa Rosada across the open plaza, with the obelisk-like pyramid as a foreground anchor. If you want a cleaner angle with fewer people, move a little to one side and shoot at an angle to the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pyramid low in the frame, with the facade running along the upper third. Keep your phone level so the building's horizontal lines stay straight. For a different view, try the Cabildo's first floor, which looks back across the plaza with the Casa Rosada in the background. If a fence blocks the view, move along the plaza and look for gaps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pink wall to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the pink stays soft and doesn't wash out. Hold the phone with both hands, and take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, with suggestions ranging from around 8-10am to just after sunrise, so check the light on the day. At night the building may be lit differently on national holidays.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square, but a fence is sometimes put up across it, and interior visits are not currently possible, so check the official site before you go.

name: Obelisco de Buenos Aires
label: Obelisco
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de la República' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de la República' (relation/4547632): middle (247 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1332861812: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Obelisco' (10 m across).
notes: The city's iconic obelisk on Avenida 9 de Julio.

text.description:
The Obelisco is the tall white needle at the crossing of Avenida Corrientes and Avenida 9 de Julio, and it is the shape most people picture when they think of Buenos Aires. It was built in 1936 to mark 400 years since the city's first foundation. Architect Alberto Prebisch designed it, and the German-led building team finished the concrete tower in just 31 days. It stands 67.5 metres tall. Its site was once a church dedicated to St Nicholas of Bari, where the Argentine flag was first raised in the city in 1812. An inscription on the north side records this.

It photographs well because it is so simple: one clean vertical against the sky, with wide avenues on every side. The best-known view is from Plaza de la República, beside the green 'BA' letters. The plants and lettering give you a foreground and show how big the tower is, while the traffic of Avenida 9 de Julio fills the background. For a second angle, try Avenida Corrientes at Carlos Pellegrini, where the lit Obelisco sits between theatre signs and neon. Another is a high, wide view from the Hotel Marriott, but check that public access is still allowed before you go.

Take your photos from the pavement, the crosswalks or the central islands. Do not step into the middle of the avenue for a better angle.
text.geographic_location: The Obelisco stands in the Plaza de la República, in the middle of central Buenos Aires, where Avenida Corrientes crosses the very wide Avenida 9 de Julio.
text.directions_text: Lines B, C and D of the Buenos Aires Metro have stations near the monument, linked by underground passages, so head for the Plaza de la República at the crossing of Avenida Corrientes and Avenida 9 de Julio. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the tower and the 'BA' letters sit together naturally. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the letters large in the foreground and the whole height of the tower in view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tip against the sky or for the lit Obelisco down Corrientes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de la República (in front of the monument, beside the green 'BA' letters). The Obelisco rising straight up with the green 'BA' sign in the foreground, framed by the plaza and the traffic on Avenida 9 de Julio. The tower is to your south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower on a vertical line so it does not lean. Put the 'BA' letters in the lower third and leave sky above the tip. For a different view, walk to Avenida Corrientes and Carlos Pellegrini and shoot down the avenue, with theatre marquees and neon on either side. Use the crosswalks and the central islands, and never stand in the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale concrete keeps its detail against a bright sky. At night, use night mode and brace your phone against a post or your own elbows to keep the neon sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or early evening, when the Obelisco is lit and the signs are glowing, gives the most atmosphere. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in the foreground.

text.access_note: The plaza is open public space and guides say it is free to enter at any hour, but check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside the Obelisco or onto a hotel terrace.
claims_not_in_sources: Dusk or early evening is a good time to photograph the lit Obelisco and the neon signs on Avenida Corrientes.
Early morning is usually quieter for photos in the plaza.
Ultra-wide lenses can make tall vertical structures lean unless the phone is held level.
Night mode works better when the phone is braced against something steady.

name: Caminito
label: Caminito
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Caminito' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Dr. Del Valle Iberlucea and Magallanes (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W144844726 (Caminito): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colourful tango street museum in La Boca.

text.description:
Caminito is a short, brightly painted lane of tin-fronted tenements, and it is the street most visitors to this part of Buenos Aires come to photograph. It is only about 150 m long, so the colours are packed closely together and you can see most of it in a few minutes. The classic postcard view uses a balcony in the foreground, with the painted fronts running away towards the far end of the lane.

The best photo is taken from the southeast end of the street, at the balcony corner. The balcony frames the shot, and the lane leads the eye down the picture. This is also the corner nearly every visitor wants, so expect other people in the frame. The street is busy with tango performers and vendors, which adds life to a photo but makes a clean, empty view hard to get. Arriving early gives you the best chance of fewer people.

If you want a different view, Fundación PROA looks down over the painted houses, the Riachuelo and the old iron bridges. Vuelta de Rocha shows the river bend with moored boats and the rusting Nicolás Avellaneda transporter bridge. Guides describe the corner and balcony, so check the exact spot when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: Caminito is in the La Boca area of Buenos Aires, close to the Riachuelo river and not far from Vuelta de Rocha and Fundación PROA.
text.directions_text: The simplest way is to go by taxi or hired scooter to the La Boca riverside area and ask for Caminito. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the lane with the balcony in the foreground. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the corner is too tight to fit the lane and balcony together. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as a single painted front or a performer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Dr. Del Valle Iberlucea and Magallanes (southeast end of the street, at the balcony corner). The painted tin-fronted tenements of the lane receding toward the far end, with the balcony as the framing element in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the balcony at one side of the picture, with the lane running away from it along a diagonal line. Hold the phone level so the painted fronts do not lean. If the lane is crowded, wait a moment for a gap, or take a Live Photo and choose the cleanest frame afterwards. For a wider view of the barrio, Fundación PROA is an alternative viewpoint, and Vuelta de Rocha is another for the river bend and the transporter bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the painted wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright colours do not wash out. Use portrait mode only for people, and ask performers first before photographing them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive, according to one guide. Plan your visit for daylight, as one guide advises against staying in the street after dark.

text.access_note: Caminito is a public street, but check the official site before you go for any events or restrictions.

name: Plaza de Mayo
label: Plaza de Mayo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cabildo de Buenos Aires' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cabildo de Buenos Aires' (way/293947112): middle (41 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17076039: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Plaza de Mayo' (244 m across).
notes: Historic main square, with the Pirámide de Mayo at its centre.

text.description: Plaza de Mayo is the main square of Buenos Aires, and the pink Casa Rosada, the seat of the President of Argentina, closes the view at one end. It photographs well because the plaza is wide and open, so you can fit the building, the space and the people in front of it into one frame. The square took its modern form in 1884, when a colonnade that split it in two was pulled down. In the middle stands the Pirámide de Mayo, put up in 1811 and the city's first national monument. The Cabildo, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the city hall are all on its edges. The best phone photo comes from height. The upper-floor balcony or terrace of the Cabildo gives a symmetrical view over the whole plaza with the Casa Rosada anchoring the far end. If you stay down in the square, the Pirámide de Mayo makes a good foreground for the Casa Rosada. Another option is a cleaner angle on the facade with fewer other visitors in the frame. This is a working political square where marches and protests are common, so expect crowds, barriers or stages. Be patient and take a few frames as people move. Rules for photography in some rooms of the Cabildo can be stricter, so check before you shoot indoors.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de Mayo is in the Monserrat district, in the financial heart of central Buenos Aires known as the microcentro. It sits between the Cabildo, the Casa Rosada and the Metropolitan Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Three Underground stations lie under the square: Plaza de Mayo (Line A), Catedral (Line D) and Bolívar (Line E). Come up to street level and look for the Cabildo on the west side of the plaza. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full symmetrical view. Use the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Casa Rosada and cut the empty foreground. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the balcony rail is clear of people.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Cabildo de Buenos Aires (upper-floor balcony or terrace overlooking the square). An elevated, symmetrical view across the whole plaza with the pink Casa Rosada anchoring the far end of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the Casa Rosada on the centre line so the view looks balanced. Keep the horizon level and the sides of the square even. As an alternative, shoot from down in the plaza with the Pirámide de Mayo as a foreground anchor.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Casa Rosada to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the pink facade keeps its colour. Check the glass or rail for reflections before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides disagree, with some favouring late afternoon and others early morning. Try late afternoon, when the sun is likely behind you and lights the facade, and come back in the morning if the crowds are thin.

text.access_note: The square is open public space; the Cabildo balcony is part of a museum, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The Cabildo stands on the west side of the plaza, so looking from it towards the Casa Rosada means looking east.
In late afternoon the sun is likely to be behind a photographer on the Cabildo balcony and to light the Casa Rosada facade.
Photographers can use the gridlines setting and exposure slider on most smartphones.
Marches and stages can bring barriers and crowds into the square at short notice.

name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
label: El Ateneo bookshop
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/341120136: the OpenStreetMap point 'El Ateneo Grand Splendid'.
notes: Former theatre turned bookshop.

text.description:
El Ateneo Grand Splendid is a working bookshop inside a former theatre on Santa Fe Avenue. The building opened in May 1919 as the Teatro Gran Splendid, designed by Peró and Torres Armengol for the impresario Max Glücksmann. It later became a cinema, and in 1929 it showed the first sound films presented in Argentina. Since the conversion around 2000, the old auditorium floor has been filled with bookshelves, and a café now sits where the stage used to be.

It photographs well because so much of the theatre is still there. Look for the painted ceiling by Nazareno Orlandi, the carved caryatids by Troiano Troiani, the crimson stage curtains and the old theatre boxes, which now hold seats for readers. The whole space is about 2,000 square metres, so you can capture it from several levels and angles. National Geographic named it the world's most beautiful bookstore in 2019.

For a good phone photo, start with one wide shot of the auditorium, then move closer for details such as the ceiling, a balcony front or the curtains. Keep your phone steady against your chest or a railing when the light is low. It is a busy shop, so wait a moment for gaps in the crowd and be considerate of people who are browsing or reading.
text.geographic_location: El Ateneo Grand Splendid is on Santa Fe Avenue in Barrio Norte, in central Buenos Aires.
text.directions_text: Head for Barrio Norte and follow Santa Fe Avenue to the shop. No nearby station is listed for this spot, so use a map app to find Santa Fe Avenue in Barrio Norte. Once you are on Santa Fe Avenue, look for the El Ateneo Grand Splendid bookshop and go inside. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full height of the auditorium, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the shelves and boxes. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the ceiling painting and the carved figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the main floor, near the middle of the room, and look towards the stage and café to see the curtains and boxes. Then turn round, or go to a higher level if you can, to look back across the room.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight, so the boxes and columns do not lean. Use the symmetry of the room by centring the stage in the frame. For a second picture, point the phone upwards to catch the ceiling frescoes, using the boxes or balcony edges as a frame. Take a few small steps to keep other visitors out of the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene, such as the stage lighting, to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly so the curtains keep their colour. If the picture looks dim or shaky, try night mode and hold still for the full capture. Portrait mode works well for a shot of a person with a bookshelf behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try a weekday morning, when it is likely to be quieter. The light inside is mostly artificial, so the time of day matters less for exposure than for the crowds.

text.access_note: This is a working bookshop and a popular visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for current opening arrangements and any rules about photography inside.

text.description:
The Mercado de San Telmo is a market in the San Telmo district of Buenos Aires, and it is a good place for relaxed, people-filled phone photos. The pictures here come from the market's character: stalls, produce and goods, shop signs, and visitors browsing in the aisles. Because you are close to everything, you can move around and try different views in a few minutes.

The phone icon on the map sits at the market itself, so you begin right at the subject. Start with a wide view of an aisle to show the space and the activity. Then move in for details such as a stall display, a hand-painted sign or a counter of goods. Look for lines that lead the eye along an aisle, and use the gridlines in your camera app to keep verticals straight.

Keep your phone close and your movements easy when it is busy. If you want a portrait of a stallholder, ask first and a smile usually helps. Wipe your lens before you start, because market interiors can be dusty or greasy.
text.geographic_location: The Mercado de San Telmo is in the San Telmo district of Buenos Aires.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way is to head for the San Telmo district by taxi or on foot and search for Mercado de San Telmo in your map app. The phone icon on the map is at the market itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. Look for the market entrance and start your photos there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most stall and aisle shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of an aisle, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details across a counter without leaning into people's space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Begin at an entrance or a wide spot in an aisle so you can see down the length of the market, then move closer to individual stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep the aisle straight and let the rows of stalls lead the eye. Include a person for scale, ideally walking away from you or turned aside. For close-ups, fill the frame with one stall's goods and keep the background soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if bright areas look washed out. In dimmer corners try night mode, holding the phone against a pillar or your chest to keep it steady. Portrait mode works well for people, with their permission.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the market is open and not too crowded so that you can move freely. Daytime gives the best natural light. Check current opening times locally before you go.

name: Café Tortoni
label: Café Tortoni
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/340141702: the OpenStreetMap point 'Café Tortoni'.
notes: Buenos Aires' oldest and most famous café.

text.description:
Café Tortoni is a famous coffeehouse on Avenida de Mayo, and it is as much a building to photograph as a place to sit down. The street front was redesigned in 1898 by the architect Alejandro Christophersen, when the entrance on Avenida de Mayo was opened. Inside, the café has kept the decoration of its early years, so the dark wood, old-fashioned fittings and the general fin de siècle feel are what you are really there to capture.

The café first opened in 1858 and takes its name from a Parisian café on Boulevard des Italiens. It moved to this site in 1880. Over the years it has welcomed writers, musicians and public figures, and the basement is now used as a stage for jazz and tango artists, which gives you a good sense of its place in the city's cultural life.

For a phone photo, start outside with the facade, then step in if you are going to have a coffee. Keep your phone's gridlines switched on so the vertical lines of the doorway and street front stay straight. Indoors, the light is usually softer and warmer, so tap on the brightest part of the scene and drag the exposure slider down a little to keep the details of the wood. Be considerate of other guests and staff when you take pictures inside, and ask if you are unsure.
text.geographic_location: Café Tortoni stands at 825 Avenida de Mayo in Buenos Aires.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so head for Avenida de Mayo in Buenos Aires and look for number 825. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, go by taxi and ask to be dropped at Café Tortoni, Avenida de Mayo 825. Once on the avenue, the phone icon on the map is at the café itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the street front and the sweep of the room, then switch to the default lens (1x) for details such as the tables and woodwork. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details on the walls and ceiling.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the facade shot, step back a little along the pavement outside so the entrance and the front fill the frame, then step inside for the interior if you are visiting.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the doorway with a vertical line so the building does not lean. Outside, stand a little back and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole front. Inside, use the default lens (1x) and look for a frame that includes tables, chairs and the old decoration together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main part of the scene, then slide the exposure down a little if bright windows or lamps wash out the picture. If the room is dim, night mode can help, but hold the phone as still as you can against a table edge or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside, daylight shows the facade best. Inside, any time the café is open works, though it is usually easier to take photos when it is less busy.

text.access_note: Café Tortoni is a working café, so access is for customers and may be restricted at busy times; check the official site before you go.

name: Palacio Barolo
label: Palacio Barolo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida de Mayo' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Avenida de Mayo nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1386044833: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palacio Barolo' (78 m across).
notes: Dante-inspired 1923 office tower on Avenida de Mayo.

text.description:
Palacio Barolo is a tall office building on Avenida de Mayo, finished in 1923 and designed by the Italian architect Mario Palanti for the businessman Luis Barolo. When it opened it was the tallest building in South America. It is 100 metres high with 22 floors, and it stayed the tallest in Buenos Aires until the Kavanagh Building took the title in the mid-1930s. The design follows Dante's Divine Comedy: the lower floors stand for hell, the middle ones for purgatory and the top ones for heaven. A lighthouse and a small spire shaped like the Southern Cross crown the tower. It was declared a national historic monument in 1997, and it still has offices, a Spanish school and a tango clothes shop.

It photographs well because the tower rises well above the lower 1920s buildings along the avenue, so it stands out clearly. The best free photo is from the pavement directly across the street, where you can fit the whole facade and tower into one frame. Stay on the pavement and watch for passers-by and traffic. Go inside only if you have a tour, as the lighthouse and rooftop views can only be reached on a scheduled guided tour. Photography is generally allowed on tours, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Palacio Barolo is at Avenida de Mayo 1370, in the Monserrat district of central Buenos Aires. It sits on the avenue among other buildings from the 1920s.
text.directions_text: We have no Underground or tram stop to give you for this spot, so head for Monserrat, the district around Avenida de Mayo, by taxi or hired scooter, and ask for Avenida de Mayo 1370. Once you are on the avenue, cross to the pavement opposite the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the whole tower fits in from the pavement across the avenue. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter shot of the facade. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the lighthouse and spire at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Avenida de Mayo (pavement directly across the street from the facade, at the building's address (Avenida de Mayo 1370)). The full tower and facade of the building, shown against the lower 1920s neighbours on the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright and level, so the tower's sides do not lean too much. Leave a little space above the spire, then use the lower neighbours as a base. If you take the guided tour, the rooftop gives a very different photo, with panoramic views over the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people and vehicles pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright daytime hour. For the rooftop views on a tour, the hour before sunset is recommended.

text.access_note: The street view is free from the public pavement, but the lighthouse and rooftop are only open on scheduled guided tours, so book ahead and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Pointing the phone upwards makes vertical lines appear to lean inwards unless the phone is held level.
Pavements and traffic on Avenida de Mayo can be busy during the day.

name: Puente de la Mujer
label: Puente de la Mujer
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puente de la Mujer' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/307155462: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Women's Bridge' (163 m long).
notes: Calatrava's white swing bridge in Puerto Madero.

text.description:
The Puente de la Mujer (Woman's Bridge) is a white footbridge across Dock 3 in Puerto Madero, designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava. A single tilted mast holds up the central span with cables. That span can swing round by 90 degrees to let boats through. Calatrava described the shape as a couple dancing the tango, and the bridge takes its name from the many Puerto Madero streets named after women. Building began in 1998 and it opened on 20 December 2001. It was declared a Cultural Heritage of the City of Buenos Aires in 2018.

It photographs well because it is one clean white shape set against the dockside towers and the water. Its curves and cables make strong lines for a phone picture, and the walkway lets you shoot along the span as well as at it. Try both ends of the bridge and the middle of the walkway, since each gives a different angle on the mast. For a wider scene, Dique 3 is a good second spot: the bridge sits there next to the old Fragata Sarmiento museum ship.

Keep your phone steady against the rail or your body when light is low. Give people crossing the bridge room, and take a few frames with and without walkers so you have a choice later.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is in Puerto Madero, the dockside commercial district of Buenos Aires. It crosses Dock 3 (Dique 3), with the dock towers behind it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for Puerto Madero and look for the Puente de la Mujer. The phone icon on the map is on the bridge itself, at the middle of the span, so once you are there you are in position. If you want a different angle, walk to either end of the span as an optional alternative. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole white arch and the towers behind it in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view along the walkway. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the mast and cables or to compress the towers behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Either end of the span is an optional alternative. From there the photo shows the white arched bridge in the foreground with the Puerto Madero towers and dock waterfront behind it. If you want the bridge alongside the Fragata Sarmiento museum ship, Dique 3 is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the mast up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Let the curve of the walkway lead the eye towards the mast. Try one shot from the bridge looking back towards the city, and another from an end of the span looking along the bridge. Dique 3 gives a different view with the museum ship beside the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little at sunset so the white structure keeps its detail and the sky stays rich. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the rail or keep your arms tucked in. Hold still until the capture finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or twilight, and after dark when the bridge is lit.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public footbridge, but check the official site before you go for any closures and for the times when the span is due to rotate.

name: Floralis Genérica
label: Floralis Genérica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de las Naciones Unidas' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de las Naciones Unidas' (way/23727108): middle (362 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/176336341: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Floralis Genérica' (25 m across).
notes: Giant steel flower sculpture in Plaza de las Naciones Unidas.

text.description:
Floralis Genérica is a giant flower made of stainless steel and aluminium, standing in United Nations Square. The architect Eduardo Catalano gave it to the city, and it dates from 2002. It is 23 m high and has six petals, and it rises out of a round reflecting pool 44 m across. That pool is the main reason it photographs well. The petals and their reflections double up, and the flower stands alone against the sky.

From here the flower is in front of you, with the Law School facade and colonnade behind it. That gives you foreground, middle and background in one shot, and it is a less common angle than the straight-on front view. If you want the petals and reflections filling the frame, walk round to the pool edge instead. For a wider view with the skyline and trees, step back a little.

The flower was designed to open in the morning and close at night, and the petals normally open at 8 and close at sunset. Some of the sculpture was damaged in a storm in December 2023, so its condition and petal movement may vary. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Floralis Genérica stands in Plaza de las Naciones Unidas, a park on Av. Pres. Figueroa Alcorta in Buenos Aires. The Law School colonnade is close by.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop (Underground, train or tram) is listed for this spot, so use the address Av. Pres. Figueroa Alcorta 2301 to find the square. Follow the paths in the square to walk round the pool. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the flower with the colonnade behind it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole pool and petals in one frame. Try 2x if you want to pull the facade closer behind the flower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de las Naciones Unidas (northwest side, near the Law School colonnade). The flower in front, with the Law School facade and colonnade behind it as a layered background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the flower on one third of the frame, so the colonnade fills the rest as a background. Keep the phone level so the columns stay straight. For a different view, walk to the pool edge for the petals and reflections, or step back for the flower against open sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the petals to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the steel does not glare. Hold the phone steady against your body or a rail for any night shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the petals are open, normally from 8 in the morning until sunset, though the timing changes with the season. Morning or late afternoon will probably suit the steel best.

text.access_note: The flower stands in an open park with paths around it, but check the official site before you go for its current state and any works.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is probably kinder to the steel surface than harsh midday sun.
Holding a phone steady against a rail or your body helps with low-light shots.

name: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
label: Metropolitan Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Mayo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Mayo' (relation/17076039): middle (244 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/265344159: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Metropolitan Cathedral' (113 m across).
notes: Neoclassical cathedral holding the mausoleum of San Martín.

text.description:
The Metropolitan Cathedral stands on the edge of Plaza de Mayo, in the middle of Buenos Aires. From the square it reads as a calm, classical front: twelve columns under a triangular pediment, with open space all around it. That openness is what makes it easy to photograph with a phone. You can stand well back and fit the whole facade into one frame, with the square in front to give it scale.

The church has a long history on this spot. When Juan de Garay founded the city in 1580, he set aside this same quarter of a city block for the main church. The building you see now is the third on the site. An earlier nave collapsed on the night of 23 May 1752, and the rebuilding that followed produced the larger church. It was declared a National Historic Monument in 1942.

For a good photo, keep the columns upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little sky above the pediment. Step to one side for a slight angle, which gives the front more depth than a straight-on shot. The facade is usually well lit at night, so an evening visit can work well. If you want a different view, the long nave looks good from the back of the church, shot wide.
text.geographic_location: In the San Nicolás neighbourhood, in the city centre of Buenos Aires. The cathedral overlooks Plaza de Mayo, on the corner of San Martín and Rivadavia streets.
text.directions_text: Head for Plaza de Mayo in the city centre (San Nicolás). Cross the open square towards the columned front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full facade with the square in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want more of the square, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns and the pediment.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Mayo. The cathedral's neoclassical facade with its twelve columns and triangular pediment, with the open square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Keep some square in the bottom of the frame to show scale. If barriers partly block the front steps, crop them out by zooming in on the columns and pediment. For a different angle, the terrace of the Casa Rosada next door is said to give higher views of the cathedral, but check access before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. At night, use night mode and brace your phone against something steady, or hold it close to your body, so the lit facade stays sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The facade is usually well lit at night, so after dark is a good option. By day, choose a time when the square is not crowded, so you can frame the front cleanly.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements; the square in front is the place for exterior photos.
claims_not_in_sources: One review says metal barriers can partly block the front steps, which may limit clear facade shots.
Services can interrupt interior photography, and a tripod may be restricted inside.
The Casa Rosada terrace is reported (single page) to give elevated views of the cathedral; whether it is open to the public or free is unconfirmed.
Plaza de Mayo is an open public square that visitors can walk across freely.
Gridlines help keep vertical lines straight, and night mode works best when the phone is braced steady (general phone advice).

name: Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires
label: MALBA
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23621021: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires (MALBA)' (89 m across).
notes: Modern Latin American art museum in Palermo.

text.description: MALBA is the Latin American art museum of Buenos Aires, on Avenida Figueroa Alcorta in the Palermo area. It opened on 21 September 2001 and was set up by the Argentine businessman Eduardo Costantini around his own collection. The museum now welcomes over a million visitors a year, so the building is a well-known landmark for the city's art scene. The design was chosen through an open competition, with 450 proposals from 45 countries. Three young Argentinian architects won first prize: Gaston Atelman, Martin Fourcade and Alfredo Tapia. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the building itself, which is a large, modern, wide shape, about 89 m across, that you can photograph as a whole from the street. The collection includes well-known works such as Frida Kahlo's Autorretrato con chango y loro (1942) and Tarsila do Amaral's Abaporu (1928). These are inside, so the outside is the place for a simple souvenir picture of your visit. Move well back from the building so the whole of it fits in, use the ultra-wide lens or panorama mode, and turn on the gridlines to keep the edges straight. Try one wide shot and one closer shot of a detail or the entrance. Rules on photography inside the galleries can differ, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: MALBA is in the Palermo district of Buenos Aires, on Avenida Figueroa Alcorta.
text.directions_text: Start from Palermo and head for Avenida Figueroa Alcorta, where the museum stands. Use a map app to navigate to Avenida Figueroa Alcorta in Palermo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the entrance or the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move out to the street side on Avenida Figueroa Alcorta, and well back from the building, until the whole of it fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them so it does not look tilted. Keep your phone level, with the sky taking up the top of the frame and some foreground at the bottom. For a second picture, move closer and shoot a section of the façade or the entrance with the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. If you want to take in the full width of the building, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a building like this, and a quieter time of day makes it easier to stand back with no one in the frame.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street, but the museum itself is a ticketed cultural venue, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.

name: Buenos Aires Japanese Garden
label: Japanese Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Puente Plano' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Puente plano Ibaraki' (way/122871571): middle (42 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W124121413 (Buenos Aires Japanese Gardens): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Landscaped Japanese garden in Palermo.

text.description: The Buenos Aires Japanese Garden is a landscaped garden built around a pond, with red bridges, a small waterfall, a vermilion torii gate on a tiny island and a tall, pagoda-like tower called the Torre de los 13 Aleros. It photographs well because these pieces sit close together and the water ties them into one scene. The best first picture is from the Puente Plano, the flat red bridge near the Hokkaido entrance. Guides describe it as the first bridge most visitors cross, and it gives the clearest first look at the garden's layout. Looking back over the pond, you can fit the arched red bridge, with its reflection behind, the waterfall on one side and the tower on the other, all in one frame. Once you have that shot, there are two good alternatives. The Puerta Torii shows the torii gate standing alone on its rock-framed island, with the water and the cultural centre behind it. The Puente Zigzag is a low, narrow crossing with the torii visible in the distance, handy for close shots of the koi. Visitors report that the garden gets crowded on weekends and sunny days, and that people sometimes stand on the path in front of the waterfall. Be patient, wait for a gap, and take a few frames rather than just one. Walk slowly and look back across the water from each bridge, because the view changes with every few steps.
text.geographic_location: The garden is in Buenos Aires.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head to the garden's entrance and follow the path inside to the pond. Inside the garden, the recommended viewpoint is the Puente Plano, the flat red bridge near the Hokkaido entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view of the pond, the arched bridge and the waterfall. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the path is busy and you want to include more of the scene. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the tower or the torii gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Puente Plano (the flat red bridge near the Hokkaido entrance, looking back over the pond toward the arched bridge). A wide view of the pond with the arched red bridge reflected behind, a small waterfall on one side and the tall pagoda-like Torre de los 13 Aleros on the other.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the arched bridge along one of the lower lines, leaving the water in the foreground so the reflection shows. Keep the waterfall and the tower at opposite edges to balance the frame. If you move on, the Puerta Torii and the Puente Zigzag make good alternatives: the first for the lone gate on its island, the second for close shots of the koi.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the red bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the reds stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone steady against the bridge rail for sharper shots. Try a Live Photo for the moving water of the waterfall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when there are fewer visitors, according to one photo guide. Weekends and sunny days are busier.

text.access_note: The garden charges an admission fee, so check the official site before you go for current opening times and ticket details.

name: Torre Monumental
label: Torre Monumental
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza San Martín' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza San Martín' (relation/531073): middle (534 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/52563680: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre de los Ingleses' (18 m across).
notes: Clock tower in Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina, near Retiro.

text.description:
Torre Monumental is a clock tower in Retiro, 75.5 m tall with eight floors. It was given to the city by Buenos Aires's British community to mark the centenary of the May Revolution, and it opened on 24 May 1916. Some people still call it Torre de los Ingleses. The design is by the English architect Ambrose Macdonald Poynter, and the tower is built in white Portland stone shipped from England. Its clock and bells were made in imitation of those at Westminster Abbey.

The tower photographs best from a distance, because you can include the setting. From across the plaza you see the tower rising above the trees, with the Sheraton hotel alongside it. The trees give you a natural frame, and the tall, narrow shape suits a portrait-orientation shot. For a closer view, walk over to the tower's own plaza, Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina. There you can look up at the base and the clock face from the terrace and the hilltop near the memorial.

The tower has had a complicated history since 1982, so you may see graffiti on it. Keep your bag closed while you take photos, as pickpocketing is a known problem around the nearby Retiro station and bus terminal.
text.geographic_location: The tower is in the Retiro district of Buenos Aires, in Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina, by Avenida San Martín and Avenida del Libertador. Plaza San Martín lies across from it.
text.directions_text: To reach the tower's own plaza and the closer views, keep walking in that direction. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower, the trees and the Sheraton in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza San Martín (across the plaza, facing the tower). The tower rising above the trees of the plaza, with the Sheraton hotel alongside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower upright against the vertical lines. Use the trees at the edges of the picture as a frame. Take one wide shot and one telephoto shot of the clock. If you have time, walk to Plaza Fuerza Aérea Argentina for a second photo looking up at the base and clock from the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the pale stone. Hold the phone level to avoid the tower leaning in the wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is likely to suit this view best, as the sun is then behind you and lights the tower's face. It is also worth going when the plaza is quieter.

text.access_note: Plaza San Martín and the tower's plaza are open public spaces, but access to the tower itself (the lift, the viewing level and the clock) varies, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cabildo of Buenos Aires
label: Cabildo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza de Mayo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza de Mayo' (relation/17076039): middle (244 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/767690911: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museo Histórico Nacional del Cabildo y de la Revolución de Mayo'.
notes: Colonial town hall on Plaza de Mayo.

text.description:
The Cabildo was the seat of Buenos Aires' town council in colonial times and later the government house of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. Today it is a museum. It photographs well because its white, arcaded front is simple and easy to read, and the open square in front of it lets you stand back and fit the whole building in. The Casa Rosada and the Pyramid of May are close by, so they can sit in the same frame or in a second shot.

The building has changed a lot over the centuries. It was handed over for use in 1748 and the tower was added in 1773, though some accounts date the tower to 1764. When Avenida de Mayo was opened in 1889, three arches were demolished, and three more went in 1931. Only five of the original arches remain. In 1939-40 the colonial look, including the tower and red roof tiles, was rebuilt from old documents using replicas, and it reopened in October 1940. It became a National Historic Monument in 1933 and a museum in 1938.

For the cleanest angle, stand on the south side of Plaza de Mayo, near the Cabildo, and shoot across the open space. Take a few frames and keep the tower upright in the shot. If you go inside, photography is generally allowed, but flash is restricted near documents and paintings.
text.geographic_location: The Cabildo stands on the edge of Plaza de Mayo in the historic centre of Buenos Aires, on Bolívar street, near the Casa Rosada and the Pyramid of May.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Plaza de Mayo in the city centre. From there the Cabildo is about 160 m to the west, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the square so the whole front and tower fit without stretching the edges. If you are close or the square is busy, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza de Mayo (south side of the square, near the Cabildo). The white colonial arcaded facade of the Cabildo framed across the open square, with the Casa Rosada and Pyramid of May nearby. The Cabildo is to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so the building does not lean. Keep the arcade and tower together, and let the open square fill the foreground. As a second angle, you can use the zoom (2x-3x) to pick out the arches and tower. For a different view, Bolívar and Avenida Presidente Julio Argentino Roca (Diagonal Sur) is a street corner a short walk away that recreates the cover of Soda Stereo's album 'Doble Vida'.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the facade keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. Take a couple of frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is suggested by a guide to the square, though that tip is really for the Casa Rosada, so the Cabildo may be less brightly lit than the pink facade.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the museum's opening hours vary and any rules for entering or taking photos inside can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing back and holding the phone level helps keep the tower upright and the lines straight.
Using the ultra-wide lens close up can stretch the edges of the building.
Plaza de Mayo can be busy, and people may walk through the frame.

name: Palacio de Aguas Corrientes
label: Aguas Corrientes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Avenida Córdoba' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Avenida Córdoba and Calle Riobamba (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1376292: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palacio de Aguas Corrientes' (146 m across).
notes: Ornate terracotta-clad water pumping station.

text.description:
The Palacio de Aguas Corrientes looks more like a grand French-style palace than a waterworks, which is much of its charm. It was built to hold the city's water tanks and was inaugurated in 1894. It still works as a pumping station. It fills a whole city block, and its walls are covered in glazed, multi-coloured terracotta tiles, more than 300,000 of them, made by Royal Doulton in Britain. Look up for the tin mansard roof and the shields of the 14 Argentine provinces of the time. It was declared a National Historic Monument in 1989.

The building photographs well because of its colour and repeating detail. The tiles pick up the light and the long facades give strong lines. The challenge is size: it is too long to fit into one frame from the pavement opposite. The best answer is the corner where Riobamba meets Córdoba. From there you can see both facades at once in a single diagonal view, which gives the building depth and avoids a flat, head-on shot. Once you have that, walk along Avenida Córdoba for a long shot of the ornate frontage. Then cross Calle Riobamba for a straight-on view of that facade.

Take a few frames of tile and shield details as well as the wide view. They tell the story of the place well. Traffic and parked vehicles can get in the way at street level, so be patient and watch for gaps.
text.geographic_location: The palace is at the northern end of the Balvanera district of Buenos Aires. It fills the block on Avenida Córdoba, with its entrance on Calle Riobamba.
text.directions_text: Head to Avenida Córdoba 1950 in the northern part of Balvanera. Walk to the northeast corner of the block, where Riobamba meets Córdoba. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the building is too big for the default lens (1x) from the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of one section. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for tiles, shields and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Avenida Córdoba and Calle Riobamba (northeast corner of the block, where Riobamba meets Córdoba). A diagonal view that takes in both the Córdoba and Riobamba facades of the terra-cotta palace in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the building parallel to the edge of the screen, so it doesn't lean. Place the corner of the palace near one of the grid lines and let the two facades lead away from it. For an alternative, walk along Avenida Córdoba for the long ornate frontage, or cross Calle Riobamba for a head-on view of that facade. Then use the telephoto for close shots of the tiles.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the terracotta colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Hold the phone level when using the ultra-wide, as the edges stretch if you tilt it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon usually shows the glazed tiles well, but any bright, clear daytime works. Avoid very harsh midday sun if you can.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public pavement; for the museum or any photography inside, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon daylight usually suits the glazed tiles.
Traffic and parked vehicles may sometimes get in the way of street-level shots.
Tilting a phone while using the ultra-wide lens exaggerates the stretching at the edges and makes vertical lines lean.

name: Argentine National Congress
label: National Congress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plaza del Congreso' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plaza del Congreso' (way/17493172): middle (235 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2468981: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Congress of Argentina' (152 m across).
notes: Domed legislature building on Plaza del Congreso.

text.description:
The Argentine National Congress is the home of the country's two chambers of parliament: a 72-seat Senate and a 257-seat Chamber of Deputies. The palace stands at the western end of Avenida de Mayo, with the Casa Rosada at the far end of the same avenue. That position helps the photograph. The building sits at the head of an open square, so you can stand back and fit the whole front into the frame.

The classic view is from Plaza del Congreso. From there you see the neoclassical facade and green dome, with the Monumento a los Dos Congresos and its sculptures in the foreground. Those sculptures give the picture depth, so it feels like more than a flat shot of a big building. A milestone marking Kilometre Zero for Argentina's national highways is also in the plaza next to the building, which makes a nice small detail shot.

The square is open, so you can move around and try a few angles. Keep the dome and the sculptures in the same frame, and wait a moment for people to walk out of the foreground. The square is sometimes busy with demonstrations and has had building work that limits access, so look at the situation when you arrive. If the front is crowded, the street corner of Hipólito Yrigoyen and Combate de los Pozos gives a street-level view of the facade and the side of the building, usually with fewer people.
text.geographic_location: The Congress is in Buenos Aires, at the western end of Avenida de Mayo, facing the Plaza del Congreso. The Casa Rosada is at the other end of the same avenue.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so get to Plaza del Congreso, at the western end of Avenida de Mayo, by whatever local transport suits you. If you are walking along Avenida de Mayo, head west with the avenue leading you straight to the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade, dome and foreground sculptures in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the details of the sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza del Congreso (front of the building, from the plaza's central fountain area looking east toward the palace). The neoclassical facade and green dome of the Congress framed by the Monumento a los Dos Congresos and its sculptures in the foreground. Face west, towards the palace, so the Monumento a los Dos Congresos and its sculptures sit in the foreground and the green dome rises behind them. One guide says a guard may let you walk up the fountain's steps for a slightly higher angle, but don't count on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome on the centre line, with the sculptures along the bottom third for depth. Keep the phone level so the columns don't lean. If the front of the plaza is crowded, try the corner of Hipólito Yrigoyen and Combate de los Pozos for a street-level view of the facade and side of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the dome keeps its colour. After dark, when the building is lit, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday. The building is also lit at night, which makes a good second visit.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square, but demonstrations and building work can limit access at times, so check conditions on the day.
